title: Key-Value Store With Load Metrics
statement:
Build an in-memory key-value store that maps string keys to string values and also measures how busy it has been recently.

The store supports four operations. Every operation carries a timestamp `t` in **milliseconds**; timestamps never decrease from one operation to the next (several operations may share the same timestamp).

- `PUT t key value`: store `value` under `key`, replacing any previous value. Prints nothing.
- `GET t key`: print the value currently stored under `key`, or `NONE` if the key was never put.
- `PUT_LOAD t`: print the load of `PUT` calls, defined below.
- `GET_LOAD t`: print the load of `GET` calls, defined below.

The **load** of an operation type at time `t` is the **average number of calls per second** of that type over the last 5 minutes. Concretely, let `c` be the number of earlier calls of that type (including the ones at exactly time `t`) whose timestamp `s` satisfies `t - 300000 < s ≤ t`. The load is `c / 300` calls per second. Print it as an exact fraction in lowest terms `a/b`; when `c = 0` print `0/1`.

A `GET` counts as a `GET` call even when the key does not exist. `PUT_LOAD` and `GET_LOAD` calls themselves are not counted as calls of any type.

Keys and values are non-empty strings of lowercase letters. Many calls can arrive within the same second or even the same millisecond, so make sure your solution handles bursts without losing precision.

**Follow-up:** the original question first used whole-second timestamps and then asked how to handle many calls that arrive within a fraction of a second (for example at 0.01 s, 0.02 s, and so on). Here this is covered by millisecond timestamps. Think about how your data structure would behave if a single timestamp received millions of calls (store a count per timestamp instead of one entry per call) and how you would bound its memory.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `q`, the number of operations.
Each of the next `q` lines is one operation in one of the forms `PUT t key value`, `GET t key`, `PUT_LOAD t` or `GET_LOAD t`.
outputFormat: Print one line for every `GET`, `PUT_LOAD` and `GET_LOAD` operation, in input order: the value or `NONE` for `GET`, and the load fraction `a/b` for the load operations. Every input contains at least one such operation.
constraints: The last operation of every input is a `GET` or a load query

examples.input:
7
PUT 1000 a x
GET 2000 a
GET 3000 b
PUT_LOAD 4000
GET_LOAD 4000
PUT_LOAD 301000
GET_LOAD 301000
examples.explanation: `GET a` returns x and `GET b` returns NONE; both count as GET calls. At time 4000 the window holds 1 PUT (load 1/300) and 2 GETs (load 2/300 = 1/150). At time 301000 the window is (1000, 301000], so the PUT at time 1000 has just expired (load 0/1), while both GETs at 2000 and 3000 are still inside (load 1/150).

examples.input:
6
PUT 10 k v
PUT 10 k w
PUT 10 j v
GET 10 k
PUT_LOAD 10
GET_LOAD 300009
examples.explanation: Three PUTs share the timestamp 10; the second overwrites key k, so the GET returns w. The PUT load is 3/300 = 1/100. At time 300009 the window is (9, 300009], so the GET at time 10 is still counted: 1/300.

hints: A hash map answers PUT and GET. For the loads you only need to know how many calls of each type fall in a sliding time window.
Timestamps never decrease, so the calls of each type form a sorted sequence. Keep one queue of timestamps per call type.
Before answering a load query at time t, pop every timestamp s with s ≤ t - 300000 from the front of that queue; the queue size is then the count c. Reduce c/300 with a gcd.
